The American water shrew (Sorex palustris) is a semi-aquatic insectivore that exhibits remarkably high metabolic demands, a trait necessitated by its active foraging lifestyle in cold streams. Respirometry trials conducted on captive individuals have measured the basal metabolic rate at 70.65 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 70.65 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animals were maintained at a core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This elevated oxygen consumption, reflecting the species' intense energetic requirements, is among the highest recorded for any mammal of its diminutive size. Newborn shrews are exceedingly small, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.5 grams [Wwb = 0.5 grams]. These altricial neonates are entirely dependent on maternal care and begin a rapid phase of growth immediately after parturition.

Following parturition, the neonatal individuals enter a critical period of dependency characterized by intense maternal investment. The gestation period of the American water shrew lasts 23 days [tg = 23 days] when the female is maintained at a body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a relatively short duration typical of small soricids. The time since birth at weaning occurs at 25 days [tx = 25 days] under the same thermal regime. By the time of weaning, the young have reached a substantial proportion of their adult size, with a wet weight at weaning of 12 grams [Wwx = 12 grams]. This period represents a critical transition from a milk-based diet to the independent capture of aquatic invertebrates, during which the mother must provision the growing litter at an enormous energetic cost.

The reproductive strategy of the American water shrew involves a relatively high investment in offspring. Females typically produce a mean of 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter], and they can complete up to 2 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 2 litters per year]. This annual reproductive output is substantial for an animal of such small body size and high metabolic rate. The maximum adult body mass attained by individuals in the wild is around 16 grams [Wwi = around 16 grams], although reported measurements range from 8 to 18 grams depending on population and seasonal conditions. Achieving this ultimate size requires efficient foraging and a consistent supply of prey, as the species does not build extensive fat reserves. The energetic demands of lactation are particularly acute, as the mother must consume prey items weighing nearly her own body mass each day to sustain her pups.

Juvenile development proceeds steadily until the onset of reproductive maturity. The time since birth at puberty in the American water shrew is estimated at 90 days [tp = 90 days] when the animals are maintained at a body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This relatively quick maturation is characteristic of small mammals with high predation risk and short life expectancies. The longevity of Sorex palustris is constrained by its high metabolic rate, with a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 547.5 days [am = approximately 547.5 days] when the animal is maintained at the typical active body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a duration that aligns with the short-lived profile of most soricids of similar size. This short life span places a premium on early and efficient reproduction, and individuals that survive through the first winter typically attempt to breed during the following spring.

The ecological role of the American water shrew as a predator of aquatic invertebrates links its life history tightly to the productivity of its stream and riparian habitat. The high metabolic rate driven by its small size and active predatory behavior means that a shrew must consume prey items totaling over half its body mass daily simply to sustain its resting metabolism. Given that foraging success is weather-dependent, the population dynamics of this species are sensitive to prolonged cold spells or floods that reduce prey availability. Shrews aggressively defend territories along stream banks, and the home range of a single individual can cover several hundred square meters. Predation by fish, owls, and larger mammalian carnivores imposes additional mortality pressure, reinforcing the selective advantage of its rapid development, short gestation, and early reproduction.
